\title{Odds-Shift Slippage in One-vs-Rest Rankers: Don't Reweight, Calibrate}

\author{Akifumi Goto}
\orcid{0009-0004-8305-6436}
\email{s6025131@st.shiga-u.ac.jp}
\affiliation{%

\begin{abstract}
Per-row top-$K$ rankers counter imbalance with a per-label positive-class weight, \texttt{scale\_pos\_weight}$=n_-/n_+$. Elkan's identity says that such a weight shifts label $j$'s log-odds by $\ln w_j$, so the model ranks by weighted odds instead of the Bayes-optimal marginal --- and that the shift can simply be inverted afterwards. What a finite learner does with a weight in the thousands, and which repair works, is unmeasured.
We call the gap between the promised shift and the realized one \emph{odds-shift slippage}. We prove that a booster whose leaf steps are capped at $c$ cannot move a label by more than $T\eta c$ nat in $T$ rounds at rate $\eta$, and we decompose the loss on Santander (\nnTest{} rows, \nnLabels{} labels) and Instacart (top-\nInLabels{} products), for LightGBM and MLP pairs differing only in the weights. On Santander $\mapseven$ falls from $\nNraw$ to $\nSraw$; the ideal odds shift explains \noddsShare\% of that fall (\nIoddsShare\% on Instacart), and per-label isotonic regression returns it to $\nSplIsoPrior$ --- but only if labels without calibration positives are mapped to their prior, not passed through. The fallback, not the calibrator, decides the sign.
The inversion is the repair that does not travel: among the weighted models of \cref{fig:regime} it pays in exactly two, those whose realized shift matched the intended one and whose cells did not saturate. Elsewhere it over-corrects or stalls, while the step bound holds in all \ncapN{} caps. Where identifiable, the realized shift tracks the intended one; saturation puts it beyond measurement on most labels. The collapse is not a property of our two benchmarks: on \nnMulan{} public MULAN datasets and \nnLearners{} learners the weighted model loses more than half its $\mapk$ in \nnCollapseCells{} of \nnDoseCells{} cells, --- \nnDelCollapseLearners{} on delicious, where every learner collapses, \nnCorelCollapseLearners{} on Corel5k and \nnOtherCollapseCells{} on genbase. Across the \nnRepairCollapseCells{} learner cells of delicious and Corel5k, per-label calibration returns the weighted model to within \nmaxRepairGapCollapse{} of the unweighted one under the same calibrator, and a shared map never comes within \nminPooledGapCollapse{} of it. Elsewhere the change at $w{=}r$ is of either sign and usually small --- \nnDoseGain{} of the remaining cells score higher with the weight than without, and the worst loses $\nmodestAnyWorst$. One caveat travels with the repair --- per-label calibration hurts where positives are scarce unless cross-validation guards it. Don't reweight, calibrate --- estimate marginals unweighted, calibrate per label with an explicit prior fallback and a rule fixed on the calibration split, then decide at top-$K$. The three steps are released as \texttt{oddslip}.
\end{abstract}

\maketitle

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Ranking many binary labels within a row is the operational core of product recommendation, tagging, and risk triage: for each customer the system scores every product, sorts, and shows the top $K$~\cite{Jain2016XMLLoss,Menon2019Reductions}. The labels are almost always imbalanced, and the most common remedy in gradient-boosting practice is a per-label positive-class weight, \texttt{scale\_pos\_weight} in XGBoost and LightGBM~\cite{Chen2016XGBoost,Ke2017LightGBM}, for which the XGBoost documentation suggests $n_-/n_+$~\cite{XGBoostDocs}; the same recipe is \texttt{pos\_weight} in binary cross-entropy for neural multi-label models.

Label-specific weights are not a free choice when the deliverable is a per-row ranking. Two facts are classical. Ranking labels by their marginal $p_{ij}=\Pr(y_{ij}=1\mid x_i)$ is Bayes-optimal for precision@$K$, and one-vs-rest training with a proper loss is consistent for it~\cite{Dembczynski2012Univariate,Menon2019Reductions,Wydmuch2018PLT}. A positive-class weight $w$ moves the population minimizer of a proper loss from $p$ to $wp/(wp+1-p)$, an odds shift by $w$~\cite{Elkan2001,Saerens2002}. Together they say that a label-specific $w_j$ makes the model rank by $w_j\cdot\mathrm{odds}(p_{ij})$, a different ranking whenever the weights differ, and the XGBoost documentation itself warns that a re-balanced model no longer predicts the right probability~\cite{XGBoostDocs}.

What the classical account leaves open is what a finite learner does when $w_j$ is in the thousands or millions, as the recommended value is for rare labels, and which post-hoc repair then works. Long-tailed recognition has reached the analogous conclusion for classification, that adjusting the classifier after unweighted training beats re-weighting the loss~\cite{Kang2020Decoupling,Menon2021LogitAdjust}, and label-shift adaptation combines calibration with a prior correction~\cite{Lipton2018LabelShift,Alexandari2020MLLS}; but both lines rank classes within one softmax, not labels across independent one-vs-rest models. Per-label isotonic regression is known to break top-$k$ accuracy in multi-class settings~\cite{Patel2021IMax}, and the extreme multi-label literature deliberately uses one shared monotone map so that precision@$k$ is untouched, deferring per-label calibration to future work~\cite{Ullah2025XMLCCalib}. Neither line measures the cross-label consequence of training weights on a top-$K$ benchmark, nor the role of the calibrator's behaviour on labels that have no calibration positives.

\Cref{fig:one} gives our answer on two product-recommendation benchmarks, Santander and Instacart, each on a pair of LightGBM models that differ only in the weights. Applying the ideal odds shift to the unweighted model reproduces only a minority of the loss the trained weighted model actually suffers. We call the remainder \emph{odds-shift slippage}: the shift the learner realizes is not the shift the weight asked for. A leaf-step cap keeps it below $\ln w_j$ (\cref{prop:budget}); without one the learner realizes between half of that shift and all of it, and only on the labels where the shift is still defined, because elsewhere cells saturate into ties that no per-label map can reorder and that no shift describes (\cref{lem:leaf}). The analytic inversion survives neither regime --- across the large-scale models, including a shared-trunk MLP on both benchmarks, it pays in exactly the two that realized the shift and saturated nothing (\cref{fig:regime}), and where it does pay on the smaller benchmarks of \cref{sec:dose} it is again where nothing saturates --- the realized shift is not measured there, so only one of the two conditions is checked --- while per-label calibration repairs the ordered part up to a small residue above the in-sample ceiling, under a deployment protocol as well. One implementation detail decides its sign: a label without calibration positives must be mapped to its prior, not passed through, or the untouched labels occupy the top of every row (\cref{prop:dead}).

\paragraph{Contributions}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,nosep]
\item \textbf{Odds-shift slippage, decomposed.} Using Elkan's identity as a what-if device we separate the top-$K$ loss of a weighted one-vs-rest ranker into the ideal odds shift, a further per-label monotone distortion (the slippage), and a residue above the in-sample per-label ceiling (\cref{fig:one}A, \cref{tab:ladder}). For the boosted pairs the shift is the minority of the loss and the slippage is the rest: \noddsShare\% on Santander and \nIoddsShare\% on Instacart, where the weight takes the ranker from $\nINraw$ to $\nISraw$. The slippage is mostly a per-label constant that differs from $\ln w_j$ (\cref{tab:ladder}, intercept-only rung; \Supp{Fig.~S1}), and the residue above the calibration ceiling is consistent with saturation ties (\cref{lem:leaf}). The share is a property of the pair rather than of the weight: on the same Santander rows an MLP pair gives up \nModdsShare\% of its loss to the same ideal shift, because its within-row logit gaps are smaller against $\ln w_j$. In the decomposition the weight is always the recommended $w_j=n_{-,j}/n_{+,j}$, which reaches \nIwMax{} on Instacart and \nwMax{} on Santander; \cref{sec:santander} adds trained $\sqrt{r}$ and $10r$ arms and \cref{sec:dose} sweeps all four magnitudes.
\item \textbf{A step budget that makes the account falsifiable.} \Cref{prop:budget} bounds the realized per-label shift of a booster with leaf-step cap $c$ by $T\eta c$ whatever the weight; two regimes follow, shortfall under a cap and saturation ties without one, and \cref{cor:exact} says the analytic inversion is exact in neither. A sweep of \ncapN{} caps on both benchmarks does not falsify the bound: every realized maximum lies inside its budget, tightly at $c=0.3$ and with room to spare at $c=5$ (\cref{fig:one}B), and no cell saturates under any cap. Nothing else is bounded, and on most labels nothing can be measured either: the realized shift is identifiable only where no cell saturates, because a clipped cell fixes it by the clipping constant rather than by the learner. Where it is identifiable, no uncapped model's \emph{median} realized shift lands more than a few per cent above the shift its weight asked for --- label by label the spread is wider, on the Instacart MLP from $\nIMSbOverLnwMin$ to $\nIMSbOverLnwMax$ --- and how much of it a model realizes depends on how the shift is estimated. The median $b_j/\ln w_j$ is $\nISbOverLnwMedian$, $\nSbOverLnwMedian$ and $\nIMSbOverLnwMedian$ for the three pairs with enough identifiable labels to report one; a clipping-free estimator, which admits any label with an unsaturated cell and so reads a larger set ($\nSnDirectShift$ and $\nISnDirectShift$ labels against $\nSnIdentShift$ and $\nISnIdentShift$), puts the two boosters at $\nSbDirectOverLnwMedian$ and $\nISbDirectOverLnwMedian$. Across both instruments the readings run from half the intended shift to $\nIMSbOverLnwMedian$ times it, and nothing lands at the several-fold overshoot a bisection run against a clipped cell reports. But on Santander that holds for \nSnIdentShift{} of \nnLabels{} labels, and the loss is carried by the rest, where the shift is undefined rather than large. \Cref{fig:regime} then shows the two conditions of \cref{cor:exact} to be jointly decisive: among the large-scale models the inversion pays for the two that realized the shift and saturated nothing, and for no other. Tie attribution sizes the saturation half directly: re-ordering only the tied cells by the unweighted model's order returns \ntieShareUnw\% of the loss on Santander and \nItieShareUnw\% on Instacart, where every row has more than $K$ cells at exactly $1.0$.
\item \textbf{Per-label calibration with a prior fallback is the repair, with its selection rule.} With labels without calibration positives mapped to their prior, per-label isotonic regression is the best post-hoc repair on every Santander base model under the test-split protocol, within $0.01$ of the in-sample ceiling, and under a deployment protocol that calibrates on a held-out validation period (\cref{tab:ladder}, \Supp{Table~S3}); a shared map repairs nothing beyond tie resolution (\cref{rem:shared}), and with the identity fallback the same calibrator lowers a direct-probability model below its raw score (\cref{prop:dead}, \Supp{Table~S1}).
On Instacart the same calibrator returns the weighted model to $\nISplIsoPrior$ (ceiling $\nISceil$) and lifts the unweighted one from $\nINraw$ to $\nINplIsoPrior$, so there the cost of the weight is the like-for-like gap after calibration, $\nINplIsoPrior-\nISplIsoPrior$, not the raw loss. Both halves of the repair reproduce outside our own data. The weight costs more than half the score in \nnCollapseCells{} of \nnDoseCells{} MULAN cells --- \nnDelCollapseLearners{} on delicious (every learner), \nnCorelCollapseLearners{} on Corel5k and \nnOtherCollapseCells{} on genbase. On the \nnRepairCollapseCells{} learner cells of delicious and Corel5k the same calibrator returns the weighted model to within \nmaxRepairGapCollapse{} of its unweighted arm and a shared map never comes within \nminPooledGapCollapse{} of it, and on Corel5k, where \ncorelDeadCalDose{} of \ncorelL{} labels have no calibration positives, the identity fallback gives $\ncorelPlIsoIdWr$ against $\ncorelPlIsoPriorWr$ for the prior on the default LightGBM --- the largest of the five learner gaps, which run down to $\ncorelIdGapMin$, so \cref{prop:dead} is visible on a public benchmark but not on every learner of it. Across \nnMulan{} MULAN benchmarks and \nnLearners{} learners the calibrator \emph{hurts} an unweighted model where calibration positives are scarce; choosing among per-label maps with a positives threshold, a shared map and no calibration by cross-validation inside the calibration split removes that harm for the default learner and fails in \nnTauSelBelowRaw{} of \nnTauCells{} cells, where the calibration split does not predict the test file (\cref{tab:mulan}, \Supp{Table~S6}). The three operations, the what-if loss, calibration with an explicit fallback, and the selection, are released as the \texttt{oddslip} library.
\end{enumerate}
All numbers are generated by one script from result files released with the paper; the dead-label policy of every calibrator is explicit.

\section{Setup and Theory}
\label{sec:theory}

Rows $i=1,\dots,n$ carry features $x_i$ and binary labels $y_{ij}$, $j=1,\dots,L$; $p_{ij}=\Pr(y_{ij}=1\mid x_i)$ is the marginal and $\pi_j=\Pr(y_{ij}=1)$ the prevalence. A scorer returns $s_{ij}$ and the system shows the $K$ largest scores of row $i$. We evaluate with $\mapk$ in the Kaggle definition (average precision at $K$ per row, averaged over rows with at least one positive) and report per-row bootstrap intervals. For precision@$K$ the population-optimal ranking sorts by $p_{ij}$, and one-vs-rest with a proper loss is consistent for it~\cite{Dembczynski2012Univariate,Koyejo2015Consistent,Menon2019Reductions}. A post-hoc calibrator is \emph{separable} if it maps label $j$ by a non-decreasing $g_j$ independently of the other labels; per-label Platt, isotonic, temperature and beta calibration~\cite{Platt1999,Zadrozny2002,Guo2017Calibration,Kull2017Beta} are separable, and so is the shared (pooled) isotonic map of~\cite{Ullah2025XMLCCalib} with $g_j\equiv g$. A positive-class weight $w_j>0$ multiplies the loss of the positives of label $j$ (\texttt{scale\_pos\_weight}, \texttt{pos\_weight}).

\begin{remark}[Shared maps never invert, distinct maps can]
\label{rem:shared}
If $g_1=\dots=g_L$ the calibrator never creates a strict inversion within a row, so a shared map is rank-neutral up to ties and can repair nothing beyond tie resolution. If two continuous maps differ at an interior point, some row's strict order is inverted. Both halves are folklore (\cref{app:proof}); shared class-wise binning~\cite{Patel2021IMax}, intra-order-preserving maps~\cite{Rahimi2020IntraOrder} and the shared map of~\cite{Ullah2025XMLCCalib} rely on the first. A per-label map can reorder, and in the population limit it should: calibrated per-label maps return the marginals. Per-label calibration therefore hurts only through estimation error, whose boundary case is a label without calibration positives (\cref{prop:dead}).
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[Odds shift, after Elkan]
\label{prop:odds}
Let $q_{ij}$ be the population minimizer of a strictly proper binary loss with positive-class weight $w_j$. Then $\operatorname{logit}q_{ij}=\operatorname{logit}p_{ij}+\ln w_j$~\cite{Elkan2001,Saerens2002}, and for $p_{ij}>p_{ik}$ the weighted scores reverse the pair iff $\operatorname{logit}p_{ij}-\operatorname{logit}p_{ik}<\ln w_k-\ln w_j$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The weighted loss is the unweighted loss under the tilted distribution whose posterior odds are $w_j$ times the original; the flip condition is the difference of the shifted logits.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
\label{cor:odds}
(a) A common weight $w_j\equiv w$ is a shared map and never changes within-row order. (b) The flipped pairs, hence the top-$K$ loss of the \emph{ideal} weighted model, depend only on the unweighted logit gaps and the intended weights, so they can be computed from an unweighted model before weighted training (\emph{what-if}); this describes a learner that realizes the shift exactly, not necessarily the one a finite learner produces. (c) When $w_jp_{ij}\ll1$, $q_{ij}\approx w_jp_{ij}$, so weighted training approximates the optimal ranking for a propensity-weighted precision@$K$ with propensities $1/w_j$~\cite{Jain2016XMLLoss}: training weights silently change the metric. If a utility-weighted ranking is wanted, multiplying calibrated marginals by the utilities is exact.
\end{corollary}

\begin{lemma}[Leaf saturation]
\label{lem:leaf}
For weighted log-loss the optimal constant in a tree leaf with $n_+$ positives and $n_-$ negatives is $\rho(w)=wn_+/(wn_++n_-)$. Any leaf with $n_+\ge1$ satisfies $\rho(w)\ge1-n_-/(wn_+)$, so its prediction is within $\varepsilon$ of one once $w\ge n_-/(\varepsilon n_+)$; all test cells routed to such leaves tie near one and lose their order across those leaves.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
$-wn_+\ln\rho-n_-\ln(1-\rho)$ is minimized at $\rho=wn_+/(wn_++n_-)$, and $1-\rho=n_-/(wn_++n_-)\le n_-/(wn_+)$.
\end{proof}

The lemma is exact for a single tree whose leaf values are weighted class frequencies and describes the fixed point that a boosted ensemble approaches when it fits the weighted objective well; it is the tree analogue of importance weights losing their effect on a flexible learner~\cite{Byrd2019}. With the recommended $w_j\approx1/\pi_j$ and leaves of at most $m_-$ negatives, every positive-containing leaf of a label with $\pi_j\le\varepsilon/m_-$ is within $\varepsilon$ of one. Two consequences follow and should be kept apart. The realized shift is no longer the constant $\ln w_j$ of \cref{prop:odds}, so the analytic inversion $q\mapsto q/(q+w(1-q))$ stops working, but the distortion is still monotone within each label, so a per-label monotone map fitted on calibration data can undo it. And the cells tied at one within a label have lost their mutual order, which no separable map recovers; this part is bounded by the gap between the in-sample per-label ceiling and the unweighted model.

\begin{proposition}[Step budget bounds the realized shift]
\label{prop:budget}
Fix label $j$. Let the weighted and the unweighted booster start from the same initial score $F_0=\operatorname{logit}\hat\pi_j$, and let each of $T$ rounds add a tree whose leaf values are clipped to $[-c,c]$ and scaled by $\eta$ (\texttt{max\_delta\_step}$=c$). Then for every $x$, $|F^{w}_j(x)-\operatorname{logit}\hat\pi_j|\le T\eta c$ and $|F^{0}_j(x)-\operatorname{logit}\hat\pi_j|\le T\eta c$, hence $|F^{w}_j(x)-F^{0}_j(x)|\le 2T\eta c$; and the label-free prevalence-matching shift $b_j$, defined by $\frac1n\sum_i\sigma(F^{w}_j(x_i)-b_j)=\hat\pi_j$, satisfies $|b_j|\le T\eta c$. Consequently, if $T\eta c<\ln w_j$, the intended shift is unrealizable: $b_j<\ln w_j$, and the analytic inversion $\operatorname{logit}q-\ln w_j$ overshoots the label-free shift by at least $\ln w_j-T\eta c$, and every cell of label $j$ by at least $\ln w_j-2T\eta c$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Each round adds at most $\eta c$ in absolute value, so the first two bounds telescope. The mean of $\sigma(F^{w}_j(x_i)-b)$ over $i$ is decreasing in $b$; at $b=T\eta c$ every argument is at most $\operatorname{logit}\hat\pi_j$, so the mean is at most $\hat\pi_j$, and at $b=-T\eta c$ it is at least $\hat\pi_j$; the solution therefore lies in $[-T\eta c,T\eta c]$. The last claim compares the realized shift with the shift of \cref{prop:odds}.
\end{proof}
The shared initial score is a property of the implementation rather than an assumption we impose: LightGBM averages the labels without the positive-class weight before the first tree, and \cref{sec:santander} verifies numerically that the weighted and the unweighted booster start from the same raw score.
% The common initial score is a property of the implementation, not an assumption: LightGBM's
% BoostFromScore (src/objective/binary_objective.hpp) averages the labels with instance weights
% only, and scale_pos_weight enters the gradients alone (GetGradients); a single-leaf first tree is
% AsConstantTree(init_score) (src/boosting/gbdt.cpp). Verified numerically: results/eda.json
% init_score_check (raw score of a 1-round model with no admissible split equals logit pi_hat for
% both models). Cited in Section 3 (Data and models).

\begin{corollary}[When the inversion is exact]
\label{cor:exact}
Inverting by $\ln w_j$ returns the unweighted ranking if $F^{w}_j(x)-F^{0}_j(x)=\ln w_j$ for all $j$ and $x$, and more generally whenever the residual $\delta_j(x)=F^{w}_j(x)-F^{0}_j(x)-\ln w_j$ does not depend on $j$ within a row; pointwise equality is the case a per-label account can check. Under a cap, pointwise equality requires $\ln w_j\le 2T\eta c$ for every $j$ by \cref{prop:budget}, while the row-constant condition constrains only the spread, $\max_j\ln w_j-\min_j\ln w_j\le 4T\eta c$, which is why a common weight (\cref{cor:odds}(a)) escapes the bound entirely; without a cap the bound is vacuous and \cref{lem:leaf} applies: once $w_j\ge n_-/(\varepsilon n_+)$ in a leaf, its cells tie at $1-\varepsilon$ and no separable map recovers their order.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The inverted score of label $j$ at $x$ is $F^{0}_j(x)+\delta_j(x)$. If $\delta_j(x)$ does not depend on $j$ it shifts every label of the row equally and leaves the within-row order of $F^{0}$ unchanged; $\delta\equiv0$ is the special case. For the cap bounds, write $D_j(x)=F^{w}_j(x)-F^{0}_j(x)$, so $|D_j|\le 2T\eta c$ by \cref{prop:budget}: pointwise equality is $D_j(x)=\ln w_j$, giving $\ln w_j\le 2T\eta c$; a row-constant residual gives $\ln w_j-\ln w_k=D_j(x)-D_k(x)$, which bounds the spread by $4T\eta c$ and leaves the magnitude free.
\end{proof}

We call the gap between the shift a weight promises, $\ln w_j$, and the shift the learner realizes \emph{odds-shift slippage}, and two regimes produce it. Under a cap tight enough to bind, $b_j\le T\eta c<\ln w_j$, the realized shift falls short; no cell saturates and the inversion over-corrects by at least the shortfall. (A cap only binds where $T\eta c<\ln w_j$; at our largest it does so for \nSmdsFivefracLnwAbove\% of Santander labels and \nISmdsFivefracLnwAbove\% of Instacart's.) Without a cap nothing bounds $b_j$, and leaves saturate; on a saturated label $b_j$ is not merely large but undefined, since no finite shift moves a cell that the stored probability has already rounded to $1.0$ (\cref{sec:santander} gives the margin this corresponds to), so the inversion is left with ties that lie beyond any separable map. Where no cell saturates the shift is identified and, as \cref{sec:santander} measures, close to $\ln w_j$. A monotone map fitted per label on calibration data absorbs the ordered part of both regimes; nothing separable absorbs the ties. \Cref{prop:budget} is falsifiable, and \cref{sec:santander} tests it at \ncapN{} caps on two datasets: the budgets run from $\nSmdsPointThreeTEtaC$ to $\nSmdsFiveTEtaC$ nat and every realized maximum stays inside its own (\cref{fig:one}B).

\begin{remark}[Dead-label takeover]
\label{prop:dead}
Let label $d$ have no calibration positives and keep its raw score $s_{id}$ (identity fallback), while every calibrated label $j$ is mapped by $g_j$ with $g_j(s)\le\bar q$ for all $s$ (isotonic outputs are bounded by the largest block mean of the calibration split). If $s_{id}>\bar q$ then $d$ is ranked above every calibrated label in row $i$ regardless of $y_{id}$; with $m$ such labels, $\min(m,K)$ of the top-$K$ slots are occupied by them. The condition holds whenever raw scores are inflated relative to calibrated ones, which is the situation that motivates calibration. This is an implementation pitfall, not a property of standard libraries: of \nnSurveyImpl{} calibration implementations we examined (\Supp{Table~S7}), every one-vs-rest calibrator returns a constant or raises on a single-class split, and only MAPIE's top-label calibrator passes an unseen label through, with a warning. Our own earlier one-vs-rest loop, and any loop that catches the failure and returns the input, produces the takeover. Dead labels themselves are not exotic: a random calibration split of \ndeadFreqSantOnePctNcal{} Santander test rows leaves \ndeadFreqSantOnePct{} of \nnLabels{} labels without a positive on average, and a 30\% split of MULAN medical leaves \ndeadFreqMedicalThirty{} of \nmedL{} on average (\nmedDeadCal{} in the seed-42 split used throughout). A prior fallback ($\tilde s_{id}=\hat\pi_d$) or exclusion removes the effect; the policy should be an explicit argument of the calibrator.
\end{remark}

\section{Two Datasets, Two Learners: the Same Model With and Without Weights}
\label{sec:santander}

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig1_decomposition_mechanism.pdf}
\Description{Two panels. Panel A: horizontal bars of MAP at 7 per dataset for the unweighted model, the ideal odds-shifted model, the trained weighted model, its analytic inversion and its per-label isotonic repair. Panel B: the largest realized per-label shift against the leaf-step cap, with the step-budget line.}

Without a cap the shift runs into the search bound (triangle) and \ncapNoneSatOne\% (Santander) and \nIcapNoneSatOne\% (Instacart) of cells sit at exactly $1.0$.

\paragraph{Data and models.} The Santander Product Recommendation data~\cite{KaggleSantander2016} has \nnLabels{} products. We sort the public training file by date and cut it at fixed row-count fractions into \nnTrain{} training rows, \nnValRows{} validation rows (held out from model fitting and preceding the test period) and \nnTest{} test rows, so the boundaries fall inside a month rather than on one and the boundary months are shared across the split; both arms of every matched pair see the identical split, so the sharing cannot produce the differences we report; the label of a row is the set of products added in the following month, and $\mapseven$ follows the Kaggle definition on the rows with at least one added product (\nfracRowsWithPos\% of the \nnEvalRows{} evaluation rows; the public leaderboard counts rows without additions as zero, so its values are not comparable). Three base scorers produce test probabilities for every cell. \Sm and \Nm are LightGBM one-vs-rest models trained by one script in one session with \emph{identical} configuration (60 trees, learning rate $0.05$, 31 leaves, no feature or row subsampling, one seed, the same feature pipeline and split); the only difference is that \Sm sets $w_j=n_{-,j}/n_{+,j}$ per label (between \nwMin{} and \nwMax) and \Nm sets no weight. An earlier run of the weighted configuration (\Supp{Table~S4}) differs from \Sm by $\nSorigMinusS$ in raw $\mapseven$ and behaves the same on every rung. \Wm (Wasserstein gradient boosting, WGBoost~\cite{Matsubara2024WGBoost}) estimates Beta-distributed probabilities directly without weights. An earlier unweighted LightGBM run with 100 trees and feature and row subsampling (\Nhm) is reported in \Supp{Table~S2} as a robustness check. Two calibration protocols are used. The \emph{test-split} protocol fits calibrators on a random 30\% of the test rows (seed 42, \nnVal{} rows) and evaluates on the remaining 70\%; it is optimistic for deployment because the calibration rows come from the test period, and its gain on the unweighted model ($\nciNprior$) bounds what the protocol itself contributes. The \emph{deployment} protocol fits calibrators on the held-out validation period and evaluates on all test rows (\Supp{Table~S3}). Under the test-split protocol \nSnDead{} labels have no positives in the calibration split and every calibrated label has at least \ncalPosMinAlive{} (median \ncalPosMedAlive). Bootstrap intervals use $B=\nbootB$ per-row resamples of the \nbootN{} evaluation rows with a positive. One instrument matters for every saturation number below: predictions are stored as single-precision probabilities, so a cell ``at exactly $1.0$'' is one whose raw margin exceeds $\nsatMarginF$ nat (in double precision the same threshold would be $\nsatMarginD$). Every saturation share, tie attribution and identifiability count in this paper is therefore a property of the stored probability array --- the object a deployed ranker consumes --- and not a claim that the learner produced an infinite score. A pipeline that keeps the raw margin instead can still order those cells; a post-hoc calibrator applied to the probabilities cannot, which is the sense in which the ties are beyond a separable map.

The Instacart 2017 data~\cite{Instacart2017} has 49,688 products and, for the 131,209 users whose last order is labelled, an ordered history of prior orders. We use it as a next-order ranking task in the form of the next-basket literature (\cref{sec:related}): one row per user and reference order, features built from the orders before it only (purchase count and recency per candidate product, aisle and department counts, basket statistics; 8,320 columns), and a within-user chronological split, the third-last order for training, the second-last as the validation period and the last as the test period, 131,209 rows each; the label of a row is the set of products in the reference order. The label set is the top-\nInLabels{} products by training frequency. The rule is to keep every product with at least 20 training positives and to cut the list by frequency at the computational budget of one LightGBM fit per label and configuration (the products with at least 20 positives number more than twice the budget); the cut is recorded in the run metadata. This is not the Kaggle task, a single binary reorder model scored by F1, and the public leaderboard is not comparable.
The weights $w_j=n_{-,j}/n_{+,j}$ range from \nIwMin{} to \nIwMax{} ($\ln w_j$ from \nIlnwMin{} to \nIlnwMax); under the test-split protocol the calibration split has \nInVal{} rows, \nISnDead{} labels without calibration positives and a median of \nIcalPosMedAlive{} positives per label (minimum \nIcalPosMinAlive), and popularity ranking scores $\nIpopMAP$. The LightGBM pair uses the Santander configuration (60 trees, learning rate $0.05$, 31 leaves, no subsampling, seed 42) with and without the weight. Both boosters start from the same initial score $\operatorname{logit}\hat\pi_j$: LightGBM's \texttt{BoostFromScore} averages the labels without \texttt{scale\_pos\_weight}, and the released EDA file verifies on a one-round model that the weighted and the unweighted booster return the same raw score, which is what \cref{prop:budget} assumes.
The second learner is a shared-trunk MLP with per-label \texttt{pos\_weight}, described where its results are discussed below; on Instacart it scores all \nIMAnLabels{} products in one model, and the top-\nInLabels{} columns enter \cref{tab:ladder} while the full label set is the all-product ladder discussed with the fallback below.

\paragraph{Decomposition and repair ladder (\cref{fig:one}, \cref{tab:ladder}).} The weighted model loses $\nSloss$ $\mapseven$ against \Nm; we express every repair as the share of this loss it returns. Adding $\ln w_j$ to the logits of \Nm is the ideal weighted model of \cref{prop:odds}; it scores $\nwhatifIdeal$, changes the top-7 set of \nfracRowsChangedWhatif\% of the first $500{,}000$ rows while keeping \noverlapWhatif{} of 7 items, and accounts for \noddsShare\% of the loss (with the milder $\sqrt{w_j}$ the ideal model scores $\nwhatifHalf$; the trained $\sqrt{r}$ arm of the same configuration scores $\nSsqrtRaw$ raw and the $10r$ arm $\nStenrRaw$, so Santander carries its own dose-response, $\nNraw$ unweighted through $\nSsqrtRaw$, $\nSraw$ and $\nStenrRaw$, and per-label isotonic regression with the prior fallback repairs all three to $\nSsqrtPlIsoPrior$, $\nSplIsoPrior$ and $\nStenrPlIsoPrior$). The trained \Sm keeps only \noverlapS{} of 7 items, has \nSsatOne\% of its cells at exactly $1.0$ and \nSsatZero\% at exactly $0.0$, and the analytic inversion with the known $w_j$ returns \nelkanShare\% ($\nSelkan$). The remaining distortion is per-label and monotone, and the ladder measures its shape by what each repair reaches. An intercept-only logit shift fitted per label on the calibration split returns \noffsetShare\% ($\nSplOffsetPrior$), so for most labels the realized distortion is close to a constant --- but not the constant $\ln w_j$. \Supp{Fig.~S1} shows why label by label: the prevalence-matching shift $b_j$ equals $\ln w_j$ on the labels whose cells never saturate (median $b_j/\ln w_j=\nSbOverLnwMedian$, range $\nSbOverLnwMin$--$\nSbOverLnwMax$, over the $\nSnIdentShift$ of \nnLabels{} labels with no saturated cell), exactly as \cref{prop:odds} says, while on every other label the cells at exactly $1.0$ cannot be moved by any finite shift, so $b_j$ is not identified at all (\nnCappedShift{} labels). We solve for $b_j$ by bisection on $[-\nshiftSearchBound,\nshiftSearchBound]$ after clipping probabilities to $[\epsilon,1-\epsilon]$, so a clipped cell sits at $\pm\nshiftClipLogit$ nat and pins the solution near that bound whatever the learner did; every $b_j$ we quote therefore comes from labels with no saturated cell. Per-label Platt scaling~\cite{Platt1999} returns \nplattShare\% and beta calibration~\cite{Kull2017Beta} \nbetaShare\%; per-label isotonic regression with the prior fallback returns \nrepairShare\% ($\nSplIsoPrior$, i.e.\ \nrepairExtraShare\% beyond the odds shift) and comes within $\nSplIsoPriorCeilGap$ of the in-sample per-label ceiling ($\nSceil$). The last \ntieShare\% ($\nSceilGap$) lies above that ceiling, and the tie attribution below shows it is the saturated cells.

Three controls guard the comparison. Per-row bootstrap intervals put the gap between \Nm raw and the repaired \Sm at $\nciNminusS$, and under the same calibrator \Nm itself reaches $\nNplIsoPrior$, so the like-for-like gap is $\nNplIsoPrior-\nSplIsoPrior$. Two symptoms that no monotone map can change agree with the ladder: the mean within-label AUC (200{,}000-row subsample) is $\nNauc$ for \Nm against $\nSauc$ for \Sm, and \Sm's ceiling ($\nSceil$) sits against \Nm's raw $\nNraw$. And pooled isotonic leaves \Wm and \Nm unchanged, as \cref{rem:shared} requires, moving \Sm from $\nSraw$ to $\nSpooled$ only because pooled blocks merge tied cells and the stable sort then breaks them by label index; no strictly ordered pair is inverted. The earlier unweighted run \Nhm (100 trees, subsampling) differs from \Nm by at most $\nNhMaxAbsDiff$ on any rung (\Supp{Table~S2}), so the decomposition does not hinge on the control's capacity. Capping the leaf step adds one observation to this ladder that the sweep below does not: a small cap costs capacity, since at $c=0.7$ both the ceiling ($\nSmdsaceil$) and the within-label AUC ($\nSmdsaauc$) fall below the uncapped model's ($\nSceil$ and $\nSauc$), leaving the rare labels under-fitted (\Supp{Table~S4}).

\paragraph{Instacart: the same decomposition, a larger role for the calibrator.} The Instacart pair loses $\nISloss$ ($\nINraw$ to $\nISraw$), keeping \nIoverlapS{} of 7 items of the unweighted top-7. The ideal odds shift --- $\ln w_j$ added to the unweighted model's own logits, as \cref{cor:odds}(b) defines it --- accounts for \nIoddsShare\% of that loss and already changes the top-7 of \nIfracRowsChangedWhatif\% of rows; the rest is slippage, and \cref{tab:ladder} gives the ladder. One thing differs from Santander and it matters for how the ladder is read: the same calibrator also lifts the \emph{unweighted} model, from $\nINraw$ to $\nINplIsoPrior$, because after 60 rounds at learning rate $0.05$ the scores of \nInLabels{} labels whose $\ln w_j$ spans \nIlnwMin{} to \nIlnwMax{} are not yet comparable across labels and the per-label maps supply that comparability. The cost of the weight is therefore the like-for-like gap after calibration, $\nINplIsoPrior$ against $\nISplIsoPrior$ with ceilings $\nINceil$ against $\nISceil$, not the raw loss. Per-row bootstrap intervals ($B=\nIbootB$ resamples of the \nIbootN{} evaluation rows with a positive) separate every comparison we draw: the repaired weighted model beats popularity by $\nIciSpriorMinusPop$ and its own analytic inversion by $\nIciSpriorMinusElkan$, and the gap between the unweighted \emph{raw} model and it is $\nIciNminusS$.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig2_inversion_regime.pdf}
\Description{Scatter of every trained weighted model: the median realized-over-intended per-label shift on a logarithmic horizontal axis against the share of the top-K loss that the analytic inversion returns. Every model sits at or near a ratio of one or well to its left. The small caps sit well left of one and return nothing or less; the largest Santander cap sits just left of one and returns almost all of the loss, as does the Instacart MLP just right of one; the two uncapped, saturated models sit near one on the horizontal axis but only just above zero.}
\caption{\textbf{Inverting by the known $\ln w_j$ pays only where the learner realized the shift \emph{and} no cell saturated --- the two conditions are separately necessary.} One marker per weighted model: both datasets, both learners, and each leaf-step cap. Horizontal: how much of the intended shift the learner put in, the median of $b_j/\ln w_j$ over the labels with no saturated cell, the only ones on which it is identified (\cref{sec:santander}). Vertical: what the inversion returns as a share of that model's $\mapseven$ loss against its own unweighted twin, so $100\%$ would restore the unweighted ranking. Filled markers have essentially no cell at exactly $1.0$ --- the Instacart MLP carries one on \nIMSnSatDroppedShift{} of \nInLabels{} labels --- while open ones carry the share shown. The uncapped Santander booster is the case that separates the two conditions: it realized $\nSbOverLnwMedian$ of its intended shift and the inversion still returns only \nelkanShare\%, because \ncapNoneSatOne\% of its cells sit at exactly $1.0$. Omitted: the Santander $\sqrt{r}$ and $10r$ arms and the all-product Instacart MLP, which are not part of the cap sweep; the Santander MLP, whose shift is identifiable on only \nMSnIdentShift{} of \nnLabels{} labels, and two Instacart caps whose weighted model already outscores its unweighted twin, leaving no loss to return.}

\paragraph{Mechanism: cap sweep and tie attribution (\cref{fig:one}B, \cref{fig:regime}).} Re-training the weighted configuration with \texttt{max\_delta\_step}$=c\in\{0.3,0.7,1,2,5\}$ ($T=\ncapT$ rounds, $\eta=\ncapEta$) bounds the realized shift by $T\eta c$, from $\nSmdsPointThreeTEtaC$ to $\nSmdsFiveTEtaC$ nat, against $\ln w_j$ up to $\ncapLnwMax$ on Santander and $\nIcapLnwMax$ on Instacart. \Cref{prop:budget} survives every cell of the sweep: the largest realized shift stays inside the budget at all \ncapN{} caps on both datasets, tightly at the smallest cap ($\nSmdsPointThreebPriorMax$ against $\nSmdsPointThreeTEtaC$ on Santander, $\nISmdsPointThreebPriorMax$ against the same budget on Instacart) and with room to spare at the largest ($\nSmdsFivebPriorMax$ and $\nISmdsFivebPriorMax$ against $\nSmdsFiveTEtaC$), and no label reaches the search bound. The cap also removes the saturation it is meant to remove: no cell of either dataset sits at exactly $1.0$ under any cap, against \ncapNoneSatOne\% and \nIcapNoneSatOne\% without one. What the cap does not do is make the analytic inversion work, and \cref{fig:regime} says when it would. Plotting the weighted models of the cap sweep and both MLP pairs by how much of the intended shift each realized and by what the inversion then returns, the two conditions of \cref{cor:exact} are visibly necessary and jointly sufficient: the inversion pays only for the two models that realized the shift \emph{and} saturated nothing (Santander $c=5$, raw $\nSmdsFiveraw$ to $\nSmdsFiveelkan$ against $\nNraw$ for \Nm; the Instacart MLP below), it over-corrects wherever the cap starved the shift, and it barely moves the uncapped models, whose realized shift is right but whose ties no separable map can reach. The repair does not travel down the sweep unchanged either. Per-label isotonic regression with the prior fallback is the best rung at all \nInCapsIsoBest{} Instacart caps and at \nnCapsIsoBest{} of \nnCapsRungs{} Santander caps ($\nSmdsFiveplIsoPrior$ and $\nISmdsFiveplIsoPrior$ at $c=5$), and at $c=5$ that capped weighted arm is the best Santander configuration in this paper: $\nSmdsFiveplIsoPrior$ against $\nNplIsoPrior$ for the unweighted model under the same calibrator, level with the unweighted WGBoost rung ($\nWplIsoPrior$), and $\nISmdsFiveplIsoPrior$ against $\nINplIsoPrior$ on Instacart. We report that rather than bury it, and we do not read it as evidence that the weight helps: the cap, not the weight, is the free variable, and we did not train an unweighted arm with a leaf-step cap, which is the control that would settle it. What the sweep does show is that a cap large enough to leave the shift realizable removes the failure this paper is about. Per-label isotonic regression is not best at the two smallest Santander caps: at $c=0.7$ per-label beta calibration is ahead ($\nSmdsPointSevenPlBetaPrior$ against $\nSmdsPointSevenplIsoPrior$), and at $c=0.3$ per-label isotonic regression is the worst rung of that model --- $\nSmdsPointThreeplIsoPrior$ against $\nSmdsPointThreeraw$ for doing nothing. That is not a fallback failure: the per-label isotonic map lands on its own in-sample reference ($\nSmdsPointThreeplIsoPrior$ against $\nSmdsPointThreeCeil$), and that reference sits below the raw score, so at this cap it is the separable isotonic map itself, not the dead-label policy, that costs the ranking --- while the two-parameter per-label families still beat doing nothing ($\nSmdsPointThreePlBetaPrior$). It is the same scarcity that \cref{sec:dose} finds on the small MULAN benchmarks, and it is what the cross-validated choice among calibrators in \cref{sec:discussion} exists to catch.

The uncapped models tie instead, and how much that costs is dataset-dependent. On Santander \nStieCellsExactOne\% of cells sit at exactly $1.0$; \nStieRowsGeOne\% of rows contain at least one and \nStieRowsGeK\% at least $K$ (mean \nStieCellsPerRowMean{} per row). Re-ordering only those tied cells by the unweighted model's order returns \ntieShareUnw\% of the loss ($\nStieColumnOrder$ to $\nStieUnwOrder$) and an oracle order that reads the test labels \ntieShareOracle\% ($\nStieOracle$): on Santander the ties are the minor part and the ordered distortion is the rest, which is why per-label calibration recovers \nrepairShare\% of the loss. On Instacart the same measurement inverts. There \nIStieCellsExactOne\% of cells tie, \emph{every} row has at least $K$ of them (mean \nIStieCellsPerRowMean{} of \nInLabels{} labels), so the top-$K$ is decided entirely by how the sort breaks ties; re-ordering the tied cells by the unweighted order returns \nItieShareUnw\% of the loss ($\nIStieColumnOrder$ to $\nIStieUnwOrder$) and the oracle order reaches $\nIStieOracle$, above the unweighted model's own $\nItieNraw$. The collapse of the weighted Instacart model is therefore mostly a tie-breaking artefact of \cref{lem:leaf}: no separable map can undo it (\cref{rem:shared}), a per-label monotone map recovers what remains ordered, and a cap prevents it at training time.

\paragraph{Two learners: what an uncapped learner does with the intended shift.} A shared-trunk MLP (two hidden layers of width 256, binary cross-entropy with per-label \texttt{pos\_weight}$\in\{1,r_j\}$, 20 epochs, no early stopping, seed 42) trained on the same rows and labels shows what \cref{prop:budget} does and does not cover. Measure the realized shift on the labels where it is identified at all --- those with no saturated cell (above) --- and the two learners agree rather than differ: the booster's median $b_j/\ln w_j$ is $\nSbOverLnwMedian$ on Santander (\nSnIdentShift{} labels) and $\nISbOverLnwMedian$ on Instacart (\nISnIdentShift), the Instacart MLP's is $\nIMSbOverLnwMedian$ (\nIMSnIdentShift), and a second estimator with no bisection and no clipped cell --- the per-label median of $\operatorname{logit}\hat q-\operatorname{logit}\hat p$ over cells inside $(10^{-6},1-10^{-6})$ in both models --- gives $\nSbDirectOverLnwMedian$ (\nSnDirectShift{} labels) and $\nISbDirectOverLnwMedian$ (\nISnDirectShift). Both instruments say the same thing about the direction and neither reports a several-fold overshoot; they differ on how much of the shift is realized, because they read different label sets, and together they place an uncapped learner's median between half of the intended shift and $\nIMSbOverLnwMedian$ times it. The agreement is at the median and not label by label --- on the Instacart MLP the ratio runs from $\nIMSbOverLnwMin$ to $\nIMSbOverLnwMax$ across its identifiable labels --- but nothing approaches the several-fold overshoot that a bisection run against a clipped cell reports. What differs between the pairs is not the size of the realized shift but how much of the label set retains one: \nSnIdentShift{} of \nnLabels{} labels on the Santander booster, \nMSnIdentShift{} on the Santander MLP --- too few to quote a median, which is why that pair is absent from \cref{fig:regime} --- against \nIMSnIdentShift{} of \nInLabels{} for the Instacart MLP, which saturates on only \nIMSnSatDroppedShift{} labels. With a cap the realized shift is bounded by $T\eta c$ in all \ncapN{} cells of the sweep on both datasets, and it falls well short of $\ln w_j$ (\cref{fig:regime}), which is the shortfall regime. \Cref{prop:budget} is a statement about the cap, and that is the only place the account is tight. The four pairs also separate \cref{cor:exact} cleanly: the analytic inversion recovers the ranking in the one pair where the shift is realized and saturation is negligible (the Instacart MLP, below; \nIMSnSatDroppedShift{} of \nInLabels{} labels carry a cell at $1.0$ at all) and in no other of the four.

What the loss decomposition adds is that the \emph{same} ideal shift costs the two pairs very differently. Applying $\ln w_j$ to each unweighted model's own logits takes LightGBM from $\nNraw$ to $\nwhatifIdeal$ but the MLP from $\nMNraw$ to $\nMwhatifIdeal$, so the textbook account explains \nModdsShare\% of the MLP pair's loss against \noddsShare\% of the booster's. The share therefore measures how large $\ln w_j$ is against the unweighted model's within-row logit gaps, and is a property of the pair, not evidence about how much shift the learner realized. Everything downstream of the shift repeats: \nMSsatOne\% of the weighted MLP's cells sit at exactly $1.0$ (against \nSsatOne\% for LightGBM), the analytic inversion returns only \nMelkanShare\% of the loss ($\nMSelkan$), and per-label isotonic regression with the prior fallback lands on its in-sample ceiling ($\nMSplIsoPrior$ against $\nMSceil$) --- but that ceiling is \nMtieShare\% of the loss below the unweighted MLP's own raw score ($\nMNraw$), so the repair returns \nMrepairShare\% and the rest is beyond any separable map.

Instacart adds the case the recipe has to cover. There the \emph{unweighted} MLP never learns a within-row signal at all: its mean within-label AUC is $\nIMNauc$, below chance, and it scores $\nIMNraw$, the popularity baseline ($\nIMpopMAP$) to three decimals, because 20 epochs of unweighted cross-entropy on \nInLabels{} labels of that rarity fit the prevalences and little else. The weighted MLP does learn ($\nIMSauc$ within-label AUC) and pays for it in the cross-label scale: it scores $\nIMSraw$ raw, below popularity, with \nIMSsatOne\% of cells at exactly $1.0$. This is the one pair in the paper that satisfies the hypothesis of \cref{cor:exact}: the realized shift matches the intended one ($b_j/\ln w_j$ median $\nIMSbOverLnwMedian$ over the $\nIMSnIdentShift$ of \nInLabels{} labels with no saturated cell, the largest identifiable set of any pair here) and saturation is negligible: \nIMSsatOne\% of cells, with only \nIMSnSatDroppedShift{} of \nInLabels{} labels carrying one at all. The analytic inversion accordingly works here, and among the four matched pairs only here: it takes the weighted model from $\nIMSraw$ to $\nIMSelkan$, past the unweighted model's own $\nIMNraw$. The all-product MLP below meets the same two conditions and the inversion pays there too ($\nIMASraw$ to $\nIMASelkan$), which is the point of stating them as conditions rather than as a list of two models. Per-label isotonic regression with the prior fallback does better still ($\nIMSplIsoPrior$ against $\nIMNplIsoPrior$, ceilings $\nIMSceil$ against $\nIMNceil$), so the repair dominates the inversion even in the regime the inversion was designed for. The weight was necessary for the optimization and ruinous for the ranking until the marginals were restored, which is the conditional form of the recipe in \cref{sec:discussion}.

\paragraph{The fallback decides the sign.} With the identity fallback, per-label isotonic regression yields $\nSplIsoId$ on \Sm (\nSplIsoIdRel\% relative to raw, below the popularity baseline: $\nciSidMinusPop$ against $\npopMAP$) and lowers \Wm from $\nWraw$ to $\nWplIsoId$ (\nWplIsoIdRel\%): the \nSnDead{} dead labels keep their raw scores (mean $\nWdeadRawMean$ on \Wm) while every calibrated label shrinks to its prevalence (largest mean $\nWaliveCalMax$), so all three sit in the top 7 of \nWdeadAllRowsPct\% of rows, the takeover of \cref{prop:dead}. This is a pitfall of the calibration wrapper, not of isotonic regression; we report it because the same wrapper produced a published negative result of ours, and because \cref{sec:dose} shows that scarce calibration positives hurt even with the prior fallback, so the two effects must be kept apart. With the prior fallback the same calibrator gives $\nSplIsoPrior$ on \Sm, $\nWplIsoPrior$ on \Wm (\nWplIsoPriorRel\%, $\nciWprior$) and $\nNplIsoPrior$ on \Nm (\nNplIsoPriorRel\%, $\nciNprior$), each within $0.01$ of its ceiling ($\nSceil$, $\nWceil$, $\nNceil$); exclusion behaves like the prior. The \nSnDead{} dead labels also have no positives in the evaluation split (\nnDeadTest{} labels have none), so the prior costs nothing here; on data where a label is rare in the calibration split but alive at test time, the prior trades that label's recall for the others' precision. Per-label Platt and beta calibration repair \Sm almost as well and come within $\nNplPlattIsoGap$ and $\nNplBetaIsoGap$ of isotonic on \Nm, but leave \Wm at its raw level ($\nWplPlattPrior$) and the intercept-only shift lowers it to $\nWplOffsetPrior$: the gain on \Wm comes from label-specific non-linear maps that one- and two-parameter families cannot express.

The all-product Instacart MLP is the case where the policy decides everything, because most labels are dead. Scoring all \nIMAnLabels{} products in one model leaves \nIMASnDead{} of them without a positive in the calibration split (\nIMASnDeadVal{} in the validation period), with weights up to \nIMAwMax. There the identity fallback returns the weighted model exactly to its raw score ($\nIMASplIsoId$ against $\nIMASraw$) --- the takeover of \cref{prop:dead} at scale: the untouched labels are far more than $K$ per row and sit above the calibrated range, which is all the proposition needs --- while the prior fallback repairs it to $\nIMASplIsoPrior$ against a popularity baseline of $\nIMApopMAP$, and the deployment protocol gives $\ndepIMASplIsoPrior$. The unweighted arm of that pair again learns nothing within a row (AUC $\nIMANauc$, raw $\nIMANraw$ at the popularity level, unchanged by any calibrator), while the weighted arm reaches $\nIMASauc$: at \nIMAnLabels{} labels the weight is what makes the model learn, and the fallback is what makes the ranking usable.

\paragraph{Deployment protocol (\Supp{Table~S3}).} Fitting the calibrators on the validation period (\nnValRows{} rows, the last training months) and evaluating on all \nnTest{} test rows removes the test-period labels from calibration. Under this protocol \Sm goes from $\ndepSraw$ to $\ndepSplIsoPrior$ with per-label isotonic regression and the prior fallback (\ndepSrepairShare\% of its loss against \Nm, whose raw score is $\ndepNraw$), the intercept-only shift returns \ndepSoffsetShare\%, and \Nm changes by $\ndepNprGain$; \ndepSnDeadVal{} labels have no positives in the validation period. The repair therefore does not depend on calibrating with test-period labels: on the per-label isotonic rung the two protocols differ by at most $\nprotoMaxDiff$, so the prior shift between the validation and test periods contributes little here.
On Instacart the same protocol calibrates on each user's second-last order and evaluates on the last. It moves the weighted model from $\ndepISraw$ to $\ndepISplIsoPrior$ and the unweighted one from $\ndepINraw$ to $\ndepINplIsoPrior$, within $\ndepISCeilGap$ and $\ndepINCeilGap$ of their ceilings ($\ndepISceil$ and $\ndepINceil$), with \ndepISnDeadVal{} labels lacking positives in the validation orders; both differ from the test-split rungs of \cref{tab:ladder} by at most $\nIprotoMaxDiffPair$ and keep their order, so the ordering of the ladder does not depend on calibrating with test-period labels.

\paragraph{Draws.} Retraining both pairs on \nseedN{} independent 90\% draws of the training rows separates what is stable from what is not (mean $\pm$ SD over the draws). The quantity that moves is the weighted model's raw score: $\nseedSraw$ on Santander, a spread of the same order as the score itself, because how far each label saturates depends on which rows the draw keeps ($\nseedSsatOne\%$ of cells at exactly $1.0$). The two rungs closest to it move with it, the analytic inversion and pooled isotonic, both of which read the depth of the saturation. Everything else the paper reads off the ladder is stable. The unweighted raw score is $\nseedNraw$, the repaired weighted model $\nseedSplIsoPrior$ against a ceiling of $\nseedSceil$, the unweighted model under the same calibrator $\nseedNplIsoPrior$, and the odds share $\nseedOddsShare\%$ against the \noddsShare\% of the matched pair. Instacart is stable throughout, including its raw scores ($\nIseedSraw$ and $\nIseedNraw$, repaired $\nIseedSplIsoPrior$ and $\nIseedNplIsoPrior$, odds share $\nIseedOddsShare\%$, saturation $\nIseedSsatOne\%$). The decomposition and the ladder are therefore properties of the configuration, not of one draw; only the depth of the weighted model's collapse depends on the sample.
