\paragraph{MULAN benchmarks.} We retrain one-vs-rest models on \nnMulan{} MULAN datasets~\cite{Tsoumakas2011MULAN} with $w_j\in\{1,\sqrt{r_j},r_j,10r_j\}$, $r_j=n_{-,j}/n_{+,j}$, and \nnLearners{} learners: the \nnMulan{} are every dataset in the MULAN distribution that ships a standard train/test split except the two largest, tmc2007 and Corel16k, which we leave out for size --- a rule a reader can check against the distribution, and the only one we apply. The largest weight the sweep reaches is $\nnMulanMaxrMax$ at $w{=}r$, three orders of magnitude below Santander's, so it is a dose-response over imbalance magnitude --- but it now also covers the label counts of \cref{sec:santander}, and there it is a second test of the collapse. The learners are LightGBM in a default and a strongly regularized configuration, XGBoost, $\ell_2$-regularized logistic regression with sample weights, and a two-layer MLP with per-label \texttt{pos\_weight}. \Cref{tab:mulan} shows the default LightGBM cells and \Supp{S6} every cell. Four regularities hold.

(i) \emph{The collapse reproduces on public data.} At $w{=}r$ the raw score falls below half its unweighted value in \nnCollapseCells{} of \nnDoseCells{} learner cells, on \ncollapseDatasets{} alone: \nnDelCollapseLearners{} on delicious (every learner), \nnCorelCollapseLearners{} on Corel5k, \nnOtherCollapseCells{} on genbase. With the default LightGBM delicious goes from $\ndelRawWone$ to $\ndelRawWr$ and Corel5k from $\ncorelRawWone$ to $\ncorelRawWr$, both below their own popularity baselines ($\ndelPop$ and $\ncorelPop$), which is the shape of \cref{tab:ladder}'s $\nINraw\to\nISraw$ on a public benchmark with a standard split. The loss is between labels rather than within them: within-label AUC moves only from $\ndelAucWone$ to $\ndelAucWr$ on delicious and from $\ncorelAucWone$ to $\ncorelAucWr$ on Corel5k, so the models still order the rows of each label and have stopped comparing labels. The repair follows the same pattern: per-label isotonic regression with the prior fallback reaches $\ndelPlIsoPriorWr$ and $\ncorelPlIsoPriorWr$, at or above what the \emph{unweighted} model attains under the same calibrator ($\ndelPlIsoPriorWone$ and $\ncorelPlIsoPriorWone$), while a shared map reaches only $\ndelPooledWr$ and $\ncorelPooledWr$ and the analytic inversion only $\ndelInvWr$ and $\ncorelInvWr$. Over all \nnRepairCollapseCells{} learner cells of delicious and Corel5k the repaired weighted model is within $\nmaxRepairGapCollapse$ of its unweighted arm and the shared map is never within $\nminPooledGapCollapse$ of it. Corel5k also carries the dead-label half: \ncorelDeadCalDose{} of its \ncorelL{} labels have no calibration positives, and there the identity fallback gives $\ncorelPlIsoIdWr$ against the prior's $\ncorelPlIsoPriorWr$ --- \cref{prop:dead} outside our own data, where delicious, with \ndelDeadCalDose{} dead labels, isolates the separable repair on its own. We do not have a threshold to offer: neither quantity separates the collapsing cells alone, since enron reaches $\max r=\nenronMaxr$ without collapsing at $L=\nenronL$, and bibtex has $\nbibtexL$ labels without collapsing at $\max r=\nbibtexMaxr$ ($\nbibtexRawWone\to\nbibtexRawWr$). Both are needed, and we report the regime rather than a rule.

(ii) For the tree learners raw $\mapk$ falls with the weight magnitude on genbase and enron and, under regularization, on medical, whereas logistic regression and XGBoost on medical gain from weights ($\nmedLogregRawWone\to\nmedLogregRawWr$ and $\nmedXgbRawWone\to\nmedXgbRawWr$ at $w{=}r$); on the \nnMulanModest{} datasets with $\max r<100$ the default LightGBM change at $w{=}r$ is a fall of between $\nmodestDefaultBest$ and $\nmodestDefaultWorst$, while across the \nnLearners{} learners the sign varies and the spread widens to $\nmodestAnyWorst$ (\nmodestAnyWorstCell) and $\nmodestAnyBest$. The default-learner reading is in line with the ``class weights are benign'' reports at imbalance ratios below 70~\cite{Liu2026Resampling}; the across-learner one shows how much of that benignity is a property of the learner rather than of the imbalance.

(iii) The what-if prediction is within $0.03$ of the trained weighted model on \nnWhatifClose{} of \nnMulan{} datasets; it under-predicts the loss where the trained model saturates (genbase: $\ngenbaseDefaultWhatifWr$ predicted, $\ngenbaseDefaultRawWr$ trained, distinct scores per label \ngenbaseDistinctWone{} to \ngenbaseDistinctWr) and over-predicts it where regularization shrinks the realized shift (enron, strongly regularized: $\nenronStrongWhatifWr$ against $\nenronStrongRawWr$), and where no saturation occurs the analytic inversion recovers the unweighted ranking (enron, strongly regularized: $\nenronStrongRawWone$ at $w{=}1$, $\nenronStrongRawWr$ at $w{=}r$, $\nenronStrongInvWr$ after inversion) --- the small-data counterpart of \cref{fig:regime}. At $w{=}r$ the what-if prediction lies inside its paired bootstrap interval of the trained model on \nnWhatifCiCoversZero{} of \nnMulan{} datasets.

(iv) A collapse in the number of distinct scores per label can sink the ceiling without any cell reaching $1.0$: on medical, strongly regularized, the count falls from $\nmedStrongDistinctWone$ to $\nmedStrongDistinctWtenr$ between $w{=}1$ and $10r$, the ceiling from $\nmedStrongCeilWone$ to $\nmedStrongCeilWtenr$, and neither inversion nor calibration returns to the unweighted level --- with $\nmedStrongSatWtenr$\% of cells saturated. So on data this small the ties that defeat a separable map are reached through coarse leaves rather than through saturation. The collapse is not sufficient: on genbase, XGBoost's count falls by a factor of four ($\ngenbaseXgbDistinctWone$ to $\ngenbaseXgbDistinctWr$ at $w{=}r$) and the ceiling still holds ($\ngenbaseXgbCeilWone$ to $\ngenbaseXgbCeilWr$), the inversion recovering past the unweighted raw score ($\ngenbaseXgbInvWr$ against $\ngenbaseXgbRawWone$); on medical, where \nmedDeadCal{} of \nmedL{} labels have no calibration positives, the identity fallback loses to the prior by up to $\nmedIdVsPriorMaxGap$.

\paragraph{The negative result and the selection rule.} The sweep also contains the negative result the recipe must carry: with few calibration positives, per-label isotonic regression with the prior fallback \emph{hurts} an unweighted model. With the default LightGBM at $w{=}1$ it lowers $\mapk$ by more than $0.005$ on \nnHurtDefault{} of \nnMulan{} datasets, and on \nnHurtTauZeroCI{} of them the paired bootstrap interval excludes zero (birds $\nbirdsRawWone\to\nbirdsPlIsoPriorWone$, $\nbirdsCiTauZero$, with a median of \ncalPosMedBirds{} calibration positives per label; medical $\nmedRawWone\to\nmedPlIsoPriorWone$, $\nmedCiTauZero$, with \ncalPosMedMedical; flags $\nflagsCiTauZero$ on \nflagsNtest{} test rows is not significant), and changes it by at most $\nmaxAbsDeltaElsewhere$ elsewhere; across learners the sign varies from dataset to dataset. The median number of calibration positives does not separate the cases cleanly (genbase and enron gain slightly with \ncalPosMedGenbase{} and \ncalPosMedEnron), so no fixed threshold can be recommended.

\paragraph{The selection rule.} \Supp{Table~S6} tests the recipe's answer to that: on the calibration split alone, \ntauFolds-fold cross-validation chooses among per-label isotonic regression with positives threshold $\tau\in\{\ntauList\}$ (labels with at most $\tau$ calibration positives keep the prior), the shared map, and no calibration. For the default LightGBM at $w{=}1$ the rule keeps the raw scores on birds, medical and flags, where every calibrator hurts or is indistinguishable from raw, and keeps the per-label gains on genbase and enron ($\tau=\ngenbaseTauSel$ and $\nenronTauSel$); on no dataset does the selected candidate lose to raw with an interval excluding zero (\nnHurtAfterTau{} of \nnMulan), and on \nnTauSigGain{} of \nnMulan{} does it gain with one --- delicious, at $\tau=\ndelTauSel$, $\ndelCiTauSel$. On the small benchmarks the rule is a guard against loss rather than a source of gain, and it becomes a source of gain exactly where the labels are many enough for per-label calibration to have something to estimate. It is not infallible: across all \nnTauCells{} cells (\nnLearners{} learners, two weight settings, \nnMulan{} datasets) the selection ends more than $0.01$ below raw in \nnTauSelBelowRaw{} of them (\ntauFailCells) against \nnTauZeroBelowRaw{} for the fixed $\tau=0$ rule, and in its worst cell ($\ntauWorstSelMinusRaw$) raw and the selected candidate are indistinguishable out of fold yet differ on the test file, so the calibration split does not predict the test file there and no rule read off that split could (\Supp{S2}).

\paragraph{Leaf saturation.} Single decision trees with \texttt{class\_weight}$=\{1{:}w\}$ have leaf values equal to the weighted class frequencies, so the saturation share computed from each leaf's $(n_+,n_-)$ and $w$ equals the measured share of predictions within $10^{-3}$ of one by construction; \Supp{Tables~S8--S9} reports this implementation check and the LightGBM sweep across \texttt{min\_child\_samples} and $w\in\{1,r,10r,100r\}$. On these small datasets the saturated share of the LightGBM sweep stays below \nleafLgbmMaxSat\%, and the single-tree check reaches $\nleafTreeMaxSat$\%, and the ceiling moves only where the number of distinct scores collapses (medical, \texttt{min\_child\_samples}$=50$: ceiling $\nleafMedCeilFiftyWone$ at $w{=}1$, $\nleafMedCeilFiftyWhundred$ at $100r$). The Santander weights ($w_j$ up to \nwMax) lie far beyond this sweep, which is where the ceiling falls below the unweighted raw score.

\paragraph{Synthetic study.} With known marginals (\Supp{Table~S10}) a realizable learner (logistic regression) attains the Bayes optimum unweighted ($\nsynLRrawDeZero$ against $\nsynTrueD$), weights degrade the ranking monotonically in the spread of $\ln w_j$, and the analytic inversion restores the optimum exactly ($\nsynLRinvD$): \cref{prop:odds} is the whole story. LightGBM fails to invert at both tree counts we tried (a 30-tree, 4-leaf model: $\nsynSmallInvD$; a 300-tree, 31-leaf model: $\nsynLargeInvD$), with \nsynSmallSatD\% and \nsynLargeSatD\% of cells saturated and in-sample ceilings intact ($\nsynSmallCeilD$, $\nsynLargeCeilD$), whereas XGBoost, also a boosted tree, saturates no cell and inverts to $\nsynXgbInvD$, and the MLP inverts to $\nsynMlpInvD$. Capacity is therefore not the deciding factor; the two libraries differ in how far a leaf may move under a large weight (XGBoost's defaults bound the leaf step with $\lambda=1$ and \texttt{min\_child\_weight}$=1$ on the weighted Hessian, LightGBM's \texttt{min\_sum\_hessian\_in\_leaf} is $10^{-3}$ with no $\ell_2$ penalty), and we did not isolate which setting matters. The study reproduces the odds shift, its exact inversion and its failure under saturation; it does not reproduce a ceiling loss of the Santander size, because even where a quarter of the cells saturate the ceiling moves by about $0.01$.

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{The odds shift, and what a learner does with it.} Elkan's identity~\cite{Elkan2001} and the prior-shift correction of~\cite{Saerens2002} describe a positive-class weight as a shift of the log-odds by $\ln w$; logit adjustment applies that shift post hoc in long-tailed classification~\cite{Menon2021LogitAdjust}, label-shift adaptation combines it with calibration~\cite{Lipton2018LabelShift}, of which our label-free prevalence-matching shift is the per-label special case, and the analytic inversion of a class-weighted model~\cite{Caplin2022ClassWeights} is the repair the identity suggests. The identity describes the population minimizer. Importance weights lose their effect on learners that can fit the weighted objective~\cite{Byrd2019}; probability estimates under imbalance corrections are unreliable~\cite{Wallace2012} and, in clinical risk models, worse calibrated without better discrimination~\cite{VandenGoorbergh2022}; at imbalance ratios up to 70 a tree-ensemble study finds class weights benign once a Platt or isotonic map is fitted~\cite{Liu2026Resampling}, which is consistent with our default-learner results at $\max r<100$, though not with every learner there. For classification, long-tailed recognition settled on adjusting the classifier after unweighted training~\cite{Kang2020Decoupling,Menon2021LogitAdjust}; those methods rank classes within one softmax, whereas we rank labels across independent one-vs-rest models, where the per-label weight is the distortion. The XGBoost documentation recommends $n_-/n_+$ and warns that the probabilities are then distorted~\cite{XGBoostDocs}. None of these measures how far a finite learner realizes the shift when $w_j$ is in the thousands~\cite{Friedman2001GBM}, nor what the unrealized part does to a ranking across labels. Doing so needs two things that are cheap only once they are named: a matched pair at scale, identical but for the weight, and a label-free reading of the realized shift, for which we use the constant that returns each label's mean prediction to its training prevalence. \Cref{prop:budget} and the cap sweep then answer the first question for a capped booster and show that nothing bounds it otherwise, and the decomposition of \cref{fig:one} answers the second.

\paragraph{Consistency and top-$K$.} One-vs-rest surrogates are consistent for the rank loss~\cite{Dembczynski2012Univariate} and, with a proper loss, for precision@$k$~\cite{Menon2019Reductions}, and the precision@$k$ regret of a plug-in ranker is bounded by its marginal error~\cite{Wydmuch2018PLT}; propensity-scored metrics weight labels deliberately~\cite{Jain2016XMLLoss}, and \cref{cor:odds}(c) shows that training weights approximate such a ranking implicitly. An instance-level weight is constant within a row and rank-neutral; a label-level weight is not, which is why the marginal must be recovered before the decision.

\paragraph{Calibration versus ranking.} Post-hoc calibration~\cite{Platt1999,Zadrozny2002,NiculescuMizil2005,Kull2017Beta,Guo2017Calibration} optimizes a probability metric, and its effect on a ranking depends on whether the map is shared or class-wise: shared class-wise binning recovers the top-5 accuracy that independent per-class maps lose on ImageNet~\cite{Patel2021IMax}, intra-order-preserving maps are rank-preserving by construction~\cite{Rahimi2020IntraOrder}, and in extreme multi-label classification a shared monotone map keeps precision@$k$ untouched while per-label calibration is deferred to future work~\cite{Ullah2025XMLCCalib}. Per-class residual offsets are Bayes-optimal for reranking when the distortion is class-separable~\cite{Wang2026BeyondLA}, the case our intercept-only rung tests; recommender systems calibrate within rank groups~\cite{Sato2024TopN}; automated calibrator selection~\cite{Abdelrahman2025SmartCal} chooses by calibration error, not by the deployed ranking metric, which is why our selection rule cross-validates $\mapk$ inside the calibration split. Relative to this line our contribution is the source of the label-wise distortion (training weights), the what-if decomposition of its odds-shift part, its two slippage regimes, and the role of the dead-label fallback.

\paragraph{Next-basket recommendation and the Instacart setting.} Predicting a user's next basket from the ordered history of prior baskets, with every item scored and the list cut at a fixed $K$, is the next-basket recommendation task~\cite{Yu2016DREAM}; its benchmark canon~\cite{Li2023NBRRealityCheck} and the nearest-neighbour and repeat-aware models it compares~\cite{Hu2020TIFUKNN,Ariannezhad2022ReCANet} use the Instacart 2017 data~\cite{Instacart2017} in this form, with the last basket of each user held out~\cite{Ariannezhad2022ReCANet} and frequency-based rankers as the reference. Our Instacart experiments follow that formulation (one row per user and reference order, features from prior orders only, the last two orders as validation and test) but ask a different question: not which model predicts the next basket best, but what per-label weights do to a fixed one-vs-rest learner and which repair returns its ranking; the popularity row of \cref{tab:ladder} is the frequency baseline of that literature.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Recipe.} Five steps, in order, for a one-vs-rest ranker over many rare labels.

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,nosep]
\item \textbf{Estimate marginals with an unweighted proper loss.} If imbalance makes optimization hard, prefer a weight common to all labels, which is rank-neutral by \cref{cor:odds}(a).
\item \textbf{If label-specific weights are kept, cap the leaf step.} A cap removes the saturation ties, which nothing post hoc can repair, at the price of leaving the intended shift unrealized: at the four smaller Santander caps, and at every Instacart cap, the analytic inversion is then wrong in the other direction, and calibration is what fixes the ranking (\cref{fig:regime}). At our largest Santander cap the price disappears --- a capped, calibrated weighted model was the best Santander configuration we trained ($\nSmdsFiveplIsoPrior$ against $\nNplIsoPrior$ for the unweighted LightGBM and $\nWplIsoPrior$ for unweighted WGBoost under the same calibrator); on Instacart it does not --- but we did not train an unweighted arm with the same cap, so we cannot say whether the gain belongs to the weight or to the cap, and step 1 stands on the uncapped comparison only. The cap is a design choice we did not tune, and a small one costs twice --- it under-fits rare labels, and it compresses the scores until no per-label monotone map can recover the cross-label order, so that at our smallest cap per-label isotonic regression scores below doing nothing (\cref{sec:santander}). Which is why the calibrator is chosen, not fixed, in step 5.
\item \textbf{Calibrate on a held-out split from the training period}, never from the evaluation period.
\item \textbf{Send labels without calibration positives to their prior, not through the identity.} Map every label with at most $\tau$ calibration positives to its prior; within the per-label isotonic family this choice, not the threshold or the split, decides whether the repair helps or hurts. It does not make every calibrator safe: with the same fallback, a per-label intercept-only shift still lowers \Wm{} to $\nWplOffsetPrior$ against raw $\nWraw$, and where calibration positives are merely scarce no $\tau$ makes a per-label map safe (birds, medical), which is what step 5 is for.
\item \textbf{Choose $\tau$, per-label versus shared, and whether to calibrate at all, by cross-validation inside the calibration split} (\Supp{Table~S6}): the candidates are cheap, the objective is the deployed metric, and the rule never touches test labels.
\end{enumerate}

Step 5 has one failure mode: where the calibration split does not predict the test data, the inner folds cannot expose the harm of any calibrator (\Supp{S2}), and no calibration is then the safe default for an unweighted model. The shared map is not a second safe default: it falls more than $0.01$ below raw in \nnSharedBelowRaw{} of the \nnTauCells{} cells, \nnSharedBelowRawWone{} of them unweighted, and the rule's own worst cell (\nsharedWorstCell, $\ntauWorstSelMinusRaw$) is one where it selected the shared map. A weighted model is the easy case --- per-label maps win at every calibration-split size, because a shared map cannot undo a per-label distortion --- while on the unweighted model they beat the shared map only down to a split of \ncalsizeSmallestNcalPlWins{} rows, median \ncalsizeSmallestMedPlWins{} positives per label (\Supp{Table~S5}). If a utility- or propensity-weighted ranking is wanted, multiply calibrated marginals by the utilities at decision time. Without labels, the share of cells at exactly $1.0$ and the number of distinct scores per label flag saturation and predict that the analytic inversion will fail, though not how much top-$K$ is lost.

\paragraph{Limitations.} The large-scale evidence is two recommendation benchmarks with \nnLabels{} and \nInLabels{} labels, two learner families (LightGBM one-vs-rest and a shared-trunk MLP) and one weight regime as the headline pair, $w_j=n_-/n_+$ up to \nwMax{} on Santander, with $\sqrt{r}$ and $10r$ arms of the same Santander configuration reported in \cref{sec:santander} and the MULAN sweep covering all four magnitudes on much smaller data. The MULAN sweep replicates the collapse but not its scale: its largest $r$ is $\nnMulanMaxrMax$ against \nwMax{} on Santander, and the two that carry most of it, Corel5k and delicious, have \ncorelNtestDose{} and \ndelNtestDose{} test rows (genbase is the third, on one learner), and on the majority of the sweep the change at $w{=}r$ is small and of either sign. What it establishes is that the collapse and its repair are not artefacts of our two benchmarks or of one learner library; what it cannot establish is where the boundary lies, since we can name a dataset with the label count that does not collapse (bibtex) and one with the weight spread that does not (enron), and we did not run the two largest MULAN datasets at all. The step budget of \cref{prop:budget} is a property of boosting with a leaf-step cap, and it is the only part of the account that is tight: without a cap we bound nothing, and the realized shift is measurable only where no cell saturates, which on the Santander MLP is \nMSnIdentShift{} of \nnLabels{} labels --- too few for a median, so that pair contributes no reading of the shift at all. Where the shift is identifiable the remaining three pairs agree to within a factor of $1.2$ on the prevalence-matching shift ($\nISbOverLnwMedian$ to $\nIMSbOverLnwMedian$ times $\ln w_j$), while the clipping-free estimator reads lower on the two boosters ($\nSbDirectOverLnwMedian$ and $\nISbDirectOverLnwMedian$), but we cannot say what any learner did on the saturated labels, only that no separable map can repair them. The MLP is one architecture at one width and one epoch budget, trained without early stopping; on Instacart its unweighted arm does not learn a within-row signal at all (AUC $\nIMNauc$), so that cell tests the repair, not the harm of the weight. The Instacart task is our formulation of next-order ranking over the top-\nInLabels{} products, in the form of the next-basket literature but not the Kaggle task, so its absolute scores are comparable to neither; the decomposition and the repair compare two models on the same rows and do not depend on that choice. The LightGBM configuration was fixed on Santander and not tuned for Instacart, where the unweighted model sits well below its own calibrated level ($\nINraw$ against $\nINplIsoPrior$); the pair isolates the weight, not the best Instacart model, the like-for-like gap after calibration is the quantity to read, and whether more boosting rounds would bring the unweighted raw score closer to its calibrated level is not tested here. The oracle ceiling is an empirical reference, not a bound on all post-hoc procedures: it is the best per-label isotonic fit in \emph{squared loss}, read off at $\mapk$, so a map fitted on the calibration split can and occasionally does exceed it (Santander $c{=}1$, $\nSmdsOneplIsoPrior$ against $\nSmdsOneCeil$). Row-dependent calibrators~\cite{Rahimi2020IntraOrder} are outside the separable class altogether. Per-label calibration needs calibration positives; no threshold in the median number of calibration positives separates the harmful from the harmless cases, and the cross-validated selection of \Supp{Table~S6} fails in \nnTauSelBelowRaw{} of \nnTauCells{} cells, where the calibration split does not predict the test file and no rule on that split can help. Each matched pair is a single run (LightGBM without subsampling is deterministic given the data); \nseedN{} draws of 90\% of the training rows reproduce every rung of the ladder for the two LightGBM pairs on both benchmarks (Draws, above), but the weighted model's raw score is not stable on Santander ($\nseedSraw$), so the depth of the collapse --- not the decomposition --- is sample-dependent there. The two MLP pairs are single stochastic runs at seed 42 without early stopping and were not repeated.
The test-split protocol calibrates on rows of the test period; the deployment protocol of \Supp{Table~S3} is the one to expect in practice, and on Santander the two agree to $\nprotoMaxDiff$. We ran both protocols on the boosted pairs only; the MLP pairs are evaluated under the test-split protocol alone. The label-free prevalence-matching shift is infeasible for \nnCappedShift{} of \nnLabels{} Santander labels and is not proposed as a repair. The \texttt{max\_delta\_step} sweep shows that a cap removes saturation and most of the raw loss while the analytic inversion still over-corrects at the four smaller caps; only at $c{=}5$, where the budget finally exceeds most $\ln w_j$, does the inversion recover the unweighted level ($\nSmdsFiveelkan$ against $\nNraw$). It does not tune the cap and does not show that any cap makes the inversion exact.

\paragraph{Conclusion.} Per-label class weights change the target of one-vs-rest training from the marginal to a weighted odds, and on two recommendation benchmarks the textbook odds shift is the minor part of the resulting top-$K$ loss for the boosted pairs (\noddsShare\% on Santander, \nIoddsShare\% on Instacart); the major part is odds-shift slippage, a realized shift that differs from $\ln w_j$ plus ties from saturation, which the analytic inversion cannot undo. How the two halves divide is a property of the pair, not of the weight: the same ideal shift costs an MLP pair \nModdsShare\% of its loss where it costs the booster \noddsShare\%. What the learner realizes is not the variable: where the shift is identifiable at all it is close to $\ln w_j$ ($\nISbOverLnwMedian$ to $\nIMSbOverLnwMedian$ across the three pairs that have such labels). What varies is how much of the label set saturates, and a saturated label has no realized shift to invert --- so the repair is what carries across learners and the inversion is not. Per-label calibration with a prior fallback supplies it up to the residue the ties impose, under a deployment protocol as well as under test-split calibration, and the fallback, not the calibrator, decides the sign. Where the weight is not needed for optimization, reweighting is the wrong tool; where it is --- the unweighted MLP on Instacart never leaves the popularity baseline --- it must be followed by per-label calibration before the top-$K$ decision.

\section*{Reproducibility}
All scores, calibrators, tables and figures are produced by the \texttt{code/} and \texttt{paper/} directories of the repository released with this paper (\url{https://github.com/souldrive7/dont-reweight-calibrate}), from fixed prediction arrays (SHA-256 recorded in the result files; the arrays are regenerated from the public Kaggle data by the released training scripts, one per benchmark) and the public MULAN ARFF files (content hashes recorded). Each matched pair --- LightGBM and MLP, on Santander and on Instacart --- shares the feature pipeline, the split and every training argument except the weight, and the configuration of every run, including the \nseedN{} draws and the \ncapN{} caps, is recorded in its metadata. The synthetic generator, the leaf-saturation check, the cross-validated selection and the bootstrap use fixed seeds, and the dead-label policy is a named argument of every calibrator.

\section{Shared and distinct separable maps}
\label{app:proof}
\begin{proposition}
\label{prop:sep}
Let $g_1,\dots,g_L$ be non-decreasing maps on a common interval $I$. (a) If $g_1=\dots=g_L$, the separable calibrator never creates a strict inversion: $s_{ij}>s_{ik}$ implies $\tilde s_{ij}\ge\tilde s_{ik}$, with equality only when both scores fall in the same plateau of the shared map. (b) If the maps are continuous and $g_j(a)\neq g_k(a)$ for some interior $a\in I$ and some $j\neq k$, there is a score vector whose strict within-row order is inverted.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
(a) is monotonicity. (b) Say $g_j(a)<g_k(a)$. By continuity of $g_j$ there is $b>a$ in $I$ with $g_j(b)<g_k(a)$; the row with $s_{ij}=b>a=s_{ik}$ has $\tilde s_{ij}<\tilde s_{ik}$. If no such $b$ exists because $a$ is the right endpoint, use continuity of $g_k$ to pick $b<a$ with $g_k(b)>g_j(a)$ and the row $s_{ik}=b<a=s_{ij}$.
\end{proof}
